passages.title: Pre-World War I Painters
passages.text:
For some years before the outbreak of World War I, a number of painters in different European countries developed works of art that some have described as prophetic: paintings that by challenging viewers’ habitual ways of perceiving the world of the present are thus said to anticipate a future world that would be very different. The artistic styles that they brought into being varied widely, but all these styles had in common a very important break with traditions of representational art that stretched back to the Renaissance.

So fundamental is this break with tradition that it is not surprising to discover that these artists—among them Picasso and Braque in France, Kandinsky in Germany, and Malevich in Russia—are often credited with having anticipated not just subsequent developments in the arts, but also the political and social disruptions and upheavals of the modern world that came into being during and after the war. One art critic even goes so far as to claim that it is the very prophetic power of these artworks, and not their break with traditional artistic techniques, that constitutes their chief interest and value.

No one will deny that an artist may, just as much as a writer or a politician, speculate about the future and then try to express a vision of that future through making use of a particular style or choice of imagery; speculation about the possibility of war in Europe was certainly widespread during the early years of the twentieth century. But the forward-looking quality attributed to these artists should instead be credited to their exceptional aesthetic innovations rather than to any power to make clever guesses about political or social trends. For example, the clear impression we get of Picasso and Braque, the joint founders of cubism, from their contemporaries as well as from later statements made by the artists themselves, is that they were primarily concerned with problems of representation and form and with efforts to create a far more “real” reality than the one that was accessible only to the eye. The reformation of society was of no interest to them as artists.

It is also important to remember that not all decisive changes in art are quickly followed by dramatic events in the world outside art. The case of Delacroix, the nineteenth-century French painter, is revealing. His stylistic innovations startled his contemporaries—and still retain that power over modern viewers—but most art historians have decided that Delacroix adjusted himself to new social conditions that were already coming into being as a result of political upheavals that had occurred in 1830, as opposed to other artists who supposedly told of changes still to come.

summaries.standard:
**Topic**

some pre-WWI painters in Europe who broke heavily with representational Renaissance styles and whose works some described as prophetic.

**Framework**

Challenge a Position

**Main Point**

The idea that these painters should be credited with predicting the future and primarily celebrated for that is dumb. They should primarily be celebrated for their artistic innovations.

P1 - *Introduction to topic*

We're told about a group of artists in a certain time period that set themselves apart by breaking with customary styles, and whose art was described by some as prophetic.

P2 - *The opposing position*

We're told about critics who are so impressed by the "break with tradition" in this art that they think the artists predicted not only future art but just the real world future. One dude even says, "THIS is actually the real reason we should care about this art / these artists. Their art was fine, but what's really compelling is that they kinda predicted the future."

P3 - *Author's Challenge begins*

The author concedes that artists can speculate about the future. Evidence from Picasso and Braque and their contemporaries instead shows their primary concern with representation and form, not social reform. The concession does not establish accidental prediction by every painter discussed.

*P4 - Author's Challenge continued (Delacroix example)*

Delacroix illustrates that artistic innovation need not anticipate subsequent political upheaval. His innovations are generally understood as responses to conditions already emerging after the 1830 upheavals. That distinction between response and anticipation supports the challenge to automatically treating innovative art as prophecy.

**Summary**

By the end of the first paragraph, we know the topic but not what we're doing with it.

By the end of the second paragraph, we've gotten some hints that we might be Challenging a Position because we're seeing more ****attributions**** like "these artists are *often credited" / "One art critic even goes so far as to claim*".

We're expecting a PIVOT into disagreement after that sort of attribution.

The 3rd paragraph instead begins with a concession wind-up:
*No will deny that [part of what you said is fine],* *****but ....*****

So the Most Valuable Sentence is that first Purpose Pivot (****but,**** yet, however, recently):
*But forward-looking quality should be credited to their aesthetic innovations rather than their power to guess political/social trends*.

The Pivot word helps us hear the author entering center stage. The fact that the following answer begins "for example" shows that our author is now trying to support this Big Idea.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately states the main idea of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The **central topic** of the passage was
*some European painters, pre-WWI*

The **framework** we probably used was
*Challenge Position*

Why?

The 1st paragraph just introduces us to the topic, this group of innovative, maybe even prophetic, painters. But we're not sure *why* the author wants to talk about this topic yet.

The 2nd paragraph introduces a Non-Author Point of View.
"these artists **are often credited with** ... having prophesied of the WWI modern world."
"**One art critic** even goes so far as to claim the main reason we should care about these painters/paintings is their prophetic power."

Any time in RC that we see an attribution to a non-author point of view, we wonder if / how the author will respond. Most frequently, the author's voice will enter the passage with a **Purpose Pivot**, like "But, Yet, However, Recently".

The 3rd paragraph starts with *concession* language. The author is going to partially agree with the 2nd paragraph's point of view before substantively disagreeing with it.

"No one will deny [that you're correct about X and Y], but ... c'mon. You're wrong about Z."

Our author's main point seems to be "We should not be interested in these painters / paintings primarily for their ability to predict the future. *The forward-looking quality attributed to these artists **should instead** be credited to their exceptional aesthetic innovations (not some power to make clever guesses about political or social stuff).*

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Since we have a Challenge Position passage about these pre-WWI painters, the main point should either sound like, "Critics who these these pre-WWI painters are significant because they predicted the future are mistaken", or it should sound like, "We should care more about these pre-WWI painters' exceptional aesthetic innovations than we should about any power they seemed to have to predict the future".

choices.text: Although they flourished independently, the pre–World War I European painters who developed new ways of looking at the world shared a common desire to break with the traditions of representational art.
choices.explanation:
This doesn't capture the essence of the *Challenge Position* framework at all. The author wrote a passage to fight over whether these painters should be celebrated for predicting the future or for making exceptional aesthetic innovations.

Nothing in this answer is touching on that central friction point of "power to predict future political/social stuff".

choices.text: The work of the pre–World War I European painters who developed new ways of looking at the world cannot be said to have intentionally predicted social changes but only to have anticipated new directions in artistic perception and expression.
choices.explanation:
This captures the essence of the *Challenge Position* framework.

The **position**:
these artists anticipated the political and social disruptions and upheavals of the modern world around WWI (and that is their chief interest and value to us).

The author's **challenge**:
no, these artists weren't concerned with predicting political and social stuff. they were obsessed with "problems of representation and form and efforts to create a far more *real* reality. reformation of society was of no interest". the forward-looking quality should be credited to their exceptional aesthetic innovations.

choices.text: The work of the pre–World War I European painters who developed new ways of looking at the world was important for its ability to predict social changes and its anticipation of new directions in artistic expression.
choices.explanation:
This doesn't capture the essence of the *Challenge Position* framework, because the author was disagreeing with critics who thought that the works of these painters was important for its ability to predict social changes.

Although the author leaves some room for it to be coincidentally true that some of their speculations about the future came true, she is sternly pushing back on this notion.

She rebuts that, "the forward-looking quality should be credited to their aesthetic innovations **rather than** any power to make clever guesses about political or social trends".

So the author would agree with the 2nd claim in this answer choice but disagree with the 1st claim.

This answer puts "prophetic power" and "aesthetic innovations" on equal footing, similar importance.

The author definitely wants us to think "aesthetic > prophetic".

choices.text: Art critics who believe that the work of some pre–World War I European painters foretold imminent social changes are mistaken because art is incapable of expressing a vision of the future.
choices.explanation:
In the beginning of the 3rd paragraph, the author concedes that "an artist may ... try to express a vision of a speculative future through making use of a particular style or choice of imagery".

The author wasn't saying the 2nd paragraph people were wrong to think that art is *capable* of expressing a vision of the future.

She thought they were wrong to think that *this group of painters* was interested in expressing a vision of the future.

She maintains that they were obsessed with aesthetics, and reforming/predicting society was of no interest to them.

choices.text: Art critics who believe that the work of some pre–World War I European painters foretold imminent social changes are mistaken because the social upheavals that followed World War I were impossible to predict.
choices.explanation:
The author wasn't saying the 2nd paragraph people were wrong because it was **impossible** to predict the social upheavals that followed WWI.

She thought they were wrong to think that *this group of painters* was interested in trying to predict stuff. She maintains that they were obsessed with aesthetics, and while they may have speculated about European war (which was a widespread speculation at the time), there was nothing special or important about that. We should be celebrating their forward-looking aesthetics, not celebrating their power of prophecy.

questions.prompt: The art critic mentioned in the last sentence of the second paragraph would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

explanationBlocks.heading: Support Window
explanationBlocks.body:
We only know one thing about this critic - the final sentence of the 2nd paragraph.

He thinks "it's the prophetic power of these works that is the main reason we're interested in them and value them. It's not their break with traditional artistic techniques."

So we just need to pick an answer that feels most derivable from that limited line reference.

choices.text: The supposed innovations of Picasso, Braque, Kandinsky, and Malevich were based on stylistic discoveries that had been made in the Renaissance but went unexplored for centuries.
choices.explanation:
This critic isn't quoted as saying that these artists ****didn't**** innovate. She may well believe that the artists innovated. She's just saying that's not the main reason we care about them or value them.

We care about / value them because they predicted the political / social future of the modern world.

choices.text: The work of Picasso, Braque, Kandinsky, and Malevich possessed prophetic power because these artists employed the traditional techniques of representational art with unusual skill.
choices.explanation:
Since he's saying, "We care about the prophetic power, not the break with traditional techniques", he's acknowledging that there ****was**** a break with traditional techniques. He wouldn't say "they were prophetic because they employed traditional techniques".

Our critic is saying that the prophetic power was their ability to anticipate political and social disruptions and upheavals in the modern world during / after WWI.

choices.text: The importance of the work of Picasso, Braque, Kandinsky, and Malevich is due largely to the fact that the work was stylistically ahead of its time.
choices.explanation: He's saying the opposite, "We care largely about the prophetic power, not about the break with traditional techniques (stylistically ahead of its time)."

choices.text: The prophecies embodied in the work of Picasso, Braque, Kandinsky, and Malevich were shrewd predictions based on insights into the European political situation.
choices.explanation: The critic assigns the works their chief value because of their prophetic power concerning European upheavals. This supports viewing the predictions as insightful. It does not follow that the critic was wholly unimpressed by the artists' aesthetic innovations; making prophecy chief does not make artistic innovation worthless.

choices.text: The artistic styles brought into being by Picasso, Braque, Kandinsky, and Malevich, while stylistically innovative, were of little significance to the history of post-World War I art.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: significance on art world
choices.explanation:
It's hard to say what this critic believes about the influence of these artists on post WWI art.

He says their ****chief**** interest and value is their prophetic power, but it's possible that he would still acknowledge that they are secondarily interesting / valuable because these innovations influenced post WWI art.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the statements of Picasso and Braque indicate that

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
The keywords *Picasso* and *Braque* appear in the 2nd and 3rd paragraphs, but only in the 3rd are we getting those two men's **statements**.

So the one Detail sentence we have says:
*they were primarily concerned with problems of representation and form and with efforts to create a far more "real" reality than the one that was accessible only to the eye.*

But we can throw in:
*As artists, they had no interest in reforming society.*

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Find whatever answer we can best match to either of our available detail sentences.

choices.text: they had a long-standing interest in politics
choices.explanation:
No part of our Support Window deals with 'politics'.

*- they were primarily concerned with problems of representation and form and with efforts to create a far more "real" reality than the one that was accessible only to the eye.*

*- As artists, they had no interest in reforming society.*

This answer also goes against the author's bigger point here, which is that people shouldn't be celebrating these artists as visionary sociopolitical figures.

choices.text: they worked actively to bring about social change
choices.tag: Out of Support Window: social change
choices.explanation: The passage explicitly says social reformation was of no interest to Picasso and Braque as artists. That conflicts with describing their work as active efforts to bring about social change. It is not a topic the supporting text simply fails to mention.

choices.text: their formal innovations were actually the result of chance
choices.tag: Out of Support Window: result of chance
choices.explanation:
No part of our Support Window deals with 'being the result of chance'. If anything, their formal innovations seem exhaustively thought out.

*- they were primarily concerned with problems of representation and form and with efforts to create a far more "real" reality than the one that was accessible only to the eye.*

*- As artists, they had no interest in reforming society.*

choices.text: their work was a deliberate attempt to transcend visual reality
choices.explanation:
We can find a synonym match for this in our Support Window.

*- they were primarily concerned with problems of representation and form and with **efforts to create a far more "real" reality than the one that was accessible only to the eye**.*

*- As artists, they had no interest in reforming society.*

This is a great illustration of the RC principle that *It Pays to be Stubborn*.

If we're utterly convinced that we have to match our answer to these two available supporting details, then we can do the work it takes to match up synonyms here.

choices.text: the formal aspects of their work were of little interest to them
choices.explanation:
Our Support Window is saying that they were primarily concerned with the formal aspects of their work. Reforming society was of little interest to them.

*- they were primarily concerned with problems of representation and form and with efforts to create a far more "real" reality than the one that was accessible only to the eye.*

*- As artists, they had no interest in reforming society.*

questions.prompt: The author presents the example of Delacroix in order to illustrate which one of the following claims?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body: The final paragraph first states that decisive artistic changes are not always followed by dramatic outside events. Delacroix then illustrates a different relation: his innovations responded to conditions already arising after political upheaval. The example challenges treating stylistic innovation as necessarily anticipating social change.

choices.text: Social or political changes usually lead to important artistic innovations.
choices.explanation:
Although the Delacroix example, according to the final sentence of the passage, is a case where social changes impacted an artistic innovation, that wasn't the author's main point in bringing up Delacroix and this answer is phrased way too strongly to be supported.

We don't know that sociopolitical changes ****usually**** lead to ****important**** artistic innovations.

choices.text: Artistic innovations do not necessarily anticipate social or political upheavals.
choices.explanation:
This is our best match for the first sentence of the final paragraph:
*some decisive changes in art are not followed by dramatic real world events*

This answer says
*some artistic innovations are not predicting social or political upheavals.*

This answer borrows language from the final sentence, where the author is contrasting Delacroix's situation (innovations *in response* to sociopolitical upheavals) with his opponents' characterization of the pre-WWI painters whom they believe innovated *in anticipation* of sociopolitical upheavals.

choices.text: Some European painters have used art to predict social or political changes.
choices.explanation: Delacroix is brought up as an example of an innovative painter who definitely was ****not**** anticipating future sociopolitical changes.

choices.text: Important stylistic innovations are best achieved by abandoning past traditions.
choices.explanation: The author is never suggesting an extreme opinion about how to ****best**** achieve stylistic innovations.

choices.text: Innovative artists can adapt themselves to social or political changes.
choices.explanation: This is true about Delacroix, but not why the author is talking about Delacroix. This doesn't match the first sentence of the last paragraph at all.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the contents of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
This question stem is worded differently from most **Organization** questions, but we can tell that it's an Organization question from the fact that the answers are listing out abstract ingredients, charting out the trajectory of the passage.

Since the ingredients use abstract language, it's useful to think about our Purpose / Framework (which is also abstractly worded).

This was a *Challenge Position* passage.

- The author introduces us to these pre-WWI painters.
- She tells us about how some critics interpret their work (prophetic in terms of the real world).
- She then rebuts this point of view, using the artists' own words to demonstrate that these works were primarily artistically innovative and not trying to predict any future or reform society.
- She ends by citing an example of Delacroix (from a different century), which is supposed to weaken the connection between innovative art and subsequent changes in the world.

The "shortcut" we can often take on Organization questions is to start by reading the last ingredient of the answer choice, because there usually will only be 1 or 2 answers whose final ingredient acceptably describes the ending of the passage.

choices.text: The author describes an artistic phenomenon; introduces one interpretation of this phenomenon; proposes an alternative interpretation and then supports this alternative by criticizing the original interpretation.
choices.explanation:
The final ingredient here is "supporting an alternative interpretation by criticizing the original interpretation".

That seems to describe the 3rd paragraph, where the author is supporting her alternative interpretation (this art didn't predict the world to come; it was merely full of artistic innovations).

That 3rd paragraph is "**undermining** the original interpretation", but is there any explicit criticism? Not quite.

But the final sentence of the passage does sound like it's criticizing the original:

*... as opposed to "other artists who **supposedly** told of changes to come"*

So it looks like we can match everything up here.

*The author describes an artistic phenomenon*
The first paragraph introduces us to the pre-WWI painters we're talking about.

*introduces one interpretation of the phenomenon*
In the 2nd paragraph, we learn that these artists are "often credited" with predicting political and social disruptions before/during/after the war. "One art critic goes so far as to claim" that what makes these works most important is how they predicted the future.

*proposes an alternative explanation*
The 3rd paragraph is where the author is saying, "we should mainly congratulate the forward-looking art innovations. These guys weren't trying to predict the future. Just ask them."

*supports the alternative by criticizing the original*
Again, this is the weakest part of this answer, but the 4th paragraph is trying to support the author's view, and it contains some phrases that remind us that the author is Challenging the Position of those critics in the 2nd.
- "It is also important to remember X"
- "as opposed to [this idea these critics have about] other artists [the pre-WWI artists] who **supposedly** told of changes to come".

choices.text: The author describes an artistic phenomenon; identifies the causes of that phenomenon; illustrates some of the consequences of the phenomenon and then speculates about the significance of these consequences.
choices.explanation:
There's no way to say the last paragraph (or final bits of the passage) were "speculating about the significance of consequences". So if we're using the shortcut, we'd probably not be enticed by this on a first pass.

We can agree to the 1st ingredient, because our 1st paragraph describes the artistic phenomenon of these pre-WWI painters.

Does the passage then talk about the **causes** of these pre-WWI painters? No. It shifts into the views of critics who think these painters were literally predicting the future.

The passage never really talks about the **consequences** of the pre-WWI painters' artworks either.

choices.text: The author describes an artistic phenomenon; articulates the traditional interpretation of this phenomenon; identifies two common criticisms of this view and then dismisses each of these criticisms by appeal to an example.
choices.explanation:
This has some "last ingredient" appeal because the passage ends with an appeal to an example (the Delacroix one).

The first two ingredients seem fine. The 1st paragraph describes an artistic phenomenon, and the 2nd paragraph describes a "traditional" interpretation (technically, we can't even justify that word 'traditional').

But we definitely don't have any "two common criticisms" in the 3rd paragraph. The author is presenting her own criticisms. She offers them; she definitely doesn't **dismiss** them.

choices.text: The author describes an artistic phenomenon; presents two competing interpretations of the phenomenon; dismisses both interpretations by appeal to an example and then introduces an alternative interpretation.
choices.explanation:
The last two ingredients here are scrambled.

The author introduces her alternative interpretation and **then** appeals to an example (Delacroix).

The author doesn't present and dismiss two competing interpretations.

She presents multiple **compatible** interpretations in the 2nd paragraph (they all essentially agree that "these artworks were predicting the future").

Then the author dismisses that interpretation and introduces an alternate one.

choices.text: The author describes an artistic phenomenon; identifies the causes of the phenomenon; presents an argument for the importance of the phenomenon and then advocates an attempt to recreate the phenomenon.
choices.explanation:
If we're doing the "last ingredient shortcut", we'd definitely axe this one, since the last paragraph is miles away from "advocating an attempt to recreate a phenomenon".

If we read from the start, we'd also see that "causes of phenomenon" and "argument for importance" are also missing.

questions.prompt: According to the author, the work of the pre–World War I painters described in the passage contains an example of each of the following EXCEPT:

explanationBlocks.heading: Supporting Text
explanationBlocks.body:
Although these painters are loosely referenced in the 1st paragraph, we would expect these details to come mainly from the 2nd and 3rd paragraphs (the 4th one is not about them).

Since the question stem says "according to the author", not according to the *passage*, the typical EXCEPT answer would be to name something that was in the passage, but not the author, like the idea that "the prophetic power, not their break with artistic traditions, is the chief source of their interest and value."

So let's find four answers that we can match up with something in the text (probably from the 3rd paragraph).

choices.text: an interest in issues of representation and form
choices.explanation: We get this at the end of the 3rd paragraph.

choices.text: a stylistic break with traditional art
choices.explanation: In the 3rd paragraph, the author refers to the aesthetic innovations these painters should be celebrated for, which we understand to be an affirmation of what we heard in the very first paragraph.

choices.text: the introduction of new artistic techniques
choices.explanation:
In the 3rd paragraph, the author credits these artists with "efforts to create a more 'real' reality than the one that was accessible only to the eye" via solving problems of representation and form.

At the end of the 2nd paragraph, these artists are acknowledged for their break with traditional artistic techniques, and since the author never pushes back against that and seems to echo it in the 3rd paragraph, we would assume the author would agree with this assessment.

choices.text: the ability to anticipate later artists
choices.explanation: This is discussed in the beginning of the 2nd paragraph, and again, we are inferring the author's agreement since she never pushes back against this detail.

choices.text: the power to predict social changes
choices.explanation:
The thesis of this whole passage is that "the forward-looking quality is their aesthetic innovations, rather than their power to make clever guesses about political or social trends", so we have a compelling reason to think the author would *not* believe this.

If we didn't have such strong negative support for this answer, it would be tough to sign off on (C) and (D) which are both language introduced in the 2nd paragraph and attributed to other people.

In essence, (C) / (D) / (E) were all claims made by other people, but our author only goes after this one in (E).

questions.prompt: Which one of the following characteristics of the painters discussed in the second paragraph does the author of the passage appear to value most highly?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
Since the *Clue Words* in the question stem are about what the author "views most highly", we might want to scan the text for any moments where the author is complimentary or stresses some detail.

The painters brought up in the 2nd paragraph continue to be discussed in the 3rd paragraph, so we can potentially look through both of those. Since we're searching for the ****author's**** view, it makes more sense to search the 3rd, where the author's voice entered the mix.

She concedes to the critics from P2 that the work of these artists has some "prophetic" aspects in the sense that they express a vision of the future through imagery.

But she doesn't think we should congratulate them for making "clever guesses about political or social trends". Instead, she thinks we should congratulate them for "their exceptional aesthetic innovations".

explanationBlocks.heading: Goal
explanationBlocks.body: Let's look for something like "their exceptional aesthetic innovations".

choices.text: their insights into pre–World War I politics
choices.explanation:
The author is *resisting* this idea, that these artists should be celebrated for their "clever guesses about ****political**** or social trends".

We're looking for "exceptional aesthetic innovations".

choices.text: the visionary nature of their social views
choices.explanation:
The author is *resisting* this idea, that these artists should be celebrated for their "clever guesses about political or ****social**** trends".

We're looking for "exceptional aesthetic innovations".

choices.text: their mastery of the techniques of representational art
choices.explanation: The author values exceptional aesthetic innovation, not mastery of the inherited representational techniques. Breaking with a tradition does not itself prove the painters lacked technical mastery; the point is which quality the author emphasizes.

choices.text: their ability to adjust to changing social conditions
choices.explanation: Adaptation to social change is discussed for Delacroix in the final paragraph, not as the chief value of the prewar painters identified in paragraph 2. For those painters the author emphasizes aesthetic accomplishment.

choices.text: their stylistic and aesthetic accomplishments
choices.explanation: This answer choice is our best match for "exceptional aesthetic innovations".

passages.title: Traditional Languages
passages.text:
Tribal communities in North America believe that their traditional languages are valuable resources that must be maintained. However, these traditional languages can fall into disuse when some of the effects of the majority culture on tribal life serve as barriers between a community and its traditional forms of social, economic, or spiritual interaction. In some communities the barrier has been overcome because people have recognized that language loss is serious and have taken action to prevent it, primarily through community self-teaching.

Before any community can systemically and formally teach a traditional language to its younger members, it must first document the language’s grammar; for example, a group of Northern Utes spent two years conducting a thorough analysis and classification of Northern Ute linguistic structures. The grammatical information is then arranged in sequence from the simpler to the more complex types of usage, and methods are devised to present the sequence in ways that will be most useful and appropriate to the culture.

Certain obstacles can stand in the way of developing these teaching methods. One is the difficulty a community may encounter when it attempts to write down elements (particularly the spellings of words) of a language that has been primarily oral for centuries, as is often the case with traditional languages. Sometimes this difficulty can simply be a matter of the lack of acceptable written equivalents for certain sounds in the traditional language: problems arise because of an insistence that every sound in the language have a unique written equivalent—a desirable but ultimately frustrating condition that no written language has ever fully satisfied.

Another obstacle is dialect. There may be many language traditions in a particular community; which one is to be written down and taught? The Northern Utes decided not to standardize their language, agreeing that various phonetic spellings of words would be accepted as long as their meanings were clear. Although this troubled some community members who favored Western notions of standard language writing or whose training in Western-style linguistics was especially rigid, the lack of standard orthography made sense in the context of the community’s needs. Within a year after the adoption of instruction in the Northern Ute language, even elementary school children could write and speak it effectively.

It has been argued that the attempt to write down traditional languages is misguided and unnecessary; after all, in many cases these languages have been transmitted in their oral form since their origins. Defenders of the practice counter that they are writing down their languages precisely because of a general decline in oral traditions, but they concede that languages could be preserved in their oral form if a community made every effort to eschew aspects of the majority culture that make this preservation difficult.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

The challenges and methods involved in preserving traditional tribal languages in North America.

**Framework**

Problem / Solution

**Main Point**

Traditional tribal languages in North America are under threat due to the influence of majority culture, but communities can address this challenge by documenting and teaching their languages, even while facing obstacles like writing systems and dialect differences. (The most valuable sentence appears at the end of paragraph 1: "In some communities the barrier has been overcome because people have recognized that language loss is serious and have taken action to prevent it, primarily through community self-teaching.")

**P1: The Problem of Language Loss**

Many tribal communities value their traditional languages, but these languages are threatened by cultural changes that interrupt traditional ways of life. Some communities have taken action to preserve their languages through self-teaching when they've realized the seriousness of language loss.

**P2: Documenting the Language**

Before systematically and formally teaching a traditional language to younger members, a community must first document its grammar. The example of the Northern Utes is given, who analyzed and organized their language rules to develop effective teaching methods suitable for their culture.

**P3: Challenge of Developing Teaching Methods – Writing Issues**

A big challenge in creating teaching materials is transcribing oral languages, since some sounds don't have easy written equivalents. Problems especially arise when people try to assign a unique written symbol for every sound—something no language has actually accomplished.

**P4: Challenge of Dialects and Standardization**

Another issue is deciding which dialect to teach, as communities often have multiple versions of a language. The Northern Utes chose not to standardize but to accept various spellings, as long as meanings were clear, a choice that worked well despite resistance from those trained in Western linguistic standards.

**P5: Debate over Writing vs. Oral Tradition**

Some argue that writing down these languages isn’t necessary—since they've always been oral. But supporters say writing helps preserve languages that are declining due to loss of oral traditions, though they concede oral preservation could work if the community made every effort to avoid the particular majority-culture aspects that make it difficult.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately states the main idea of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body: The first paragraph identifies the risk of losing traditional languages and introduces community self-teaching. The middle paragraphs explain grammar documentation, teaching methods and obstacles. The ending presents and answers an objection to writing languages down. The main point is the preservation programs despite difficulties; the order of speakers alone does not establish the author's personal agreement.

choices.text: In the face of the pervasive influences of the majority culture, some tribes are having difficulty teaching their traditional languages to younger tribe members.
choices.explanation:
Everything about this answer seems workable, except for the emphasis of its main clause. If we switched it from "some tribes are having difficulty teaching their traditional languages" to something like "some tribes are choosing to teach their traditional languages", then it would be fine.

As written, this answer makes it sound like the passage was primarily about the *Problem* of teaching traditional language.

In reality, the *Problem* was traditional languages are disappearing, and the *Solution* was to teach the traditional language.

Yes, there are difficult obstacles to deal with as you embark on the process of trying to teach a traditional language, but the passage doesn't spend any time talking about how *younger* tribe members are struggling to learn it.

choices.text: If tribes are to continue to hold on to their cultures in the face of majority culture influences, it is necessary for them to first teach their traditional languages to younger tribe members.
choices.explanation:
This is pretty close to the correct big picture; it's just phrased too severely.

Where can we point to that would justify saying that the author claimed that teaching traditional languages is ****necessary**** for tribes to hold on to their cultures?

The first paragraph uses much softer language:
- traditional language ****can**** fall into disuse in the face of majority culture influences
- in ****some**** communities the barrier has been overcome because they've started teaching these languages

choices.text: Responding to doubts about the value of preserving oral forms of culture, some tribes, using techniques of Western-style linguistics, have taught their traditional languages to younger tribe members.
choices.tag: Unsupported Causal Relationship / Wrong Emphasis: Western linguistics
choices.explanation:
The first clause is saying that what has caused some tribes to start teaching traditional languages is "doubts about the value of preserving oral forms of culture".

That's not what the passage identifies as the causal catalyst. The second sentence of the passage says that the background conditions prompting this were that the languages were falling into disuse because the majority culture was creating a barrier between a community and its traditional interaction.

This answer also gets weird by elevating "Western-style linguistics" to the main point, when that didn't play any central role in the passage. In fact, in the one sentence where that appears, it doesn't even appear in the ****main**** clause of that sentence.

choices.text: Recognizing the value of their traditional languages, some tribes, despite the difficulties involved, have developed programs to teach their traditional languages to younger tribe members.
choices.explanation:
The first clause nicely captures the first two sentences of the passage where we lay out the *Problem* (tribal communities believe their traditional languages are valuable resources, however, those languages are falling into disuse).

The little phrase about "despite the difficulties involved" captures the 3rd and 4th paragraphs, in which we discuss obstacles.

And the main clause, "some tribes have developed programs to teach traditional languages" sounds like it's naming the *Solution* without going over the top and saying it's 'necessary'.

choices.text: Sidestepping the inherent contradiction of preserving oral forms of culture in writing, some tribes are attempting, eschewing the influences of the majority culture, to teach their traditional languages to younger tribe members.
choices.explanation:
The main clause here is fine: some tribes are attempting to teach their traditional languages to younger tribe members. In fact, weirdly, all five answers had a main clause that was pretty much on point. So all the eliminations are about the add-ons and qualifiers.

Can we match up anything from the passage with "the inherent contradictions of preserving oral forms in writing"?

The only pushback to this endeavor comes at the start of the final paragraph, but they aren't saying, "Why are you guys trying to teach traditional languages in written form? Don't you find it contradictory to write down something oral?"

They are saying, "Why are you guys bothering to write down traditional languages? Isn't that ****unnecessary****? Haven't they been transmitted orally since their origins?"

The debate in the final paragraph isn't about whether or not it's inherently dumb to write down something oral. The debate is about whether the oral tradition is still alive and well enough to dependably carry on the traditional language.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, the first step in preparing to formally teach a traditional language is to

choices.text: analyze and classify its linguistic structures
develop a hierarchy of its grammatical information
determine appropriate methods for its presentation
search for written equivalents for each of its sounds
decide whether its syntax and spelling will be standardized

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, those who hold the view described in the first sentence of the last paragraph would be most likely to agree with which one of the following statements?

choices.text: Even if left exclusively in oral form, traditional languages are likely to survive.
There has been a decline in communication among tribal members in general.
Some oral customs do not need to be preserved orally.
External influences have little effect on tribal customs.
Tribes must focus on establishing a written tradition.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following scenarios is LEAST compatible with aspects of traditional-language preservation discussed in the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The correct answer on this question should sound like it's something that kind of goes *against* one of the things the passage highlighted as a "good thing to do" if you're trying to preserve a traditional language.

It would be pretty hard to predict this answer, and the four incorrect answers should sound like things that *were* talked about in the passage, as part of an effort to preserve a traditional language.

So we should probably just head to the answers, see if there are any that are easy to get rid of, and then research the remaining ones.

choices.text: A community decides that the best way to maintain its traditional language is to rejuvenate its oral culture.
choices.explanation: These traditional languages in many cases have been transmitted in oral form since their origins. So the cultures employing them often feel like the languages *should* be in oral form, and in the last paragraph the author is saying that "languages could be preserved in their oral form, as long as the community makes every effort" to keep the influence of the majority culture at bay.

choices.text: A community arranges the grammatical structures of its traditional language sequentially according to the degree of their complexity.
choices.explanation:
This answer seems to match up with the 2nd paragraph, where the Northern Utes are analyzed and classified linguistic structures of their traditional language:

*The grammatical information is then arranged in sequence from the simpler to the more complex types of usage*.

choices.text: A community agrees to incorporate words from the majority culture in its traditional language to make it easier to teach.
choices.explanation: The passage presents preservation through documenting and teaching the traditional language, while identifying some majority-culture effects as barriers. It never proposes incorporating majority-culture words to ease teaching. That makes this the least compatible strategy among the choices. The passage does not condemn every form of cultural borrowing or require rejecting every outside influence.

choices.text: A community determines the most appropriate methods for presenting its traditional language to students.
choices.explanation:
This answer seems to align with the last sentence of the 2nd paragraph:

*methods are devised to present the sequence (of grammatical information) in ways that will be most useful and appropriate to the culture.*

choices.text: A community deliberates about which dialect of its traditional language should be taught to students.
choices.explanation:
This aligns with what was being discussed in the 4th paragraph:

*There may be many language traditions (dialects) in a particular community; which one is to be written down and taught*?

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the organization of the passage?

choices.text: A problem is identified, followed by a list of obstacles to its solution; examples of the obstacles are discussed; a solution is proposed; methods of implementing the solution are described; an alternative to the solution is introduced and endorsed.

A problem is identified, followed by solutions to the problem; methods of implementing the solutions are discussed; obstacles to implementing the solutions are described; an alternative method of implementing one of the solutions is proposed.

A problem is identified, followed by a solution to the problem; a method of implementing the solution is discussed; obstacles to implementing the solution are described; a challenge to the solution is introduced and countered.

A problem is identified, followed by examples of the problem; a solution is proposed; a method for implementing the solution is described; examples of successful implementation are discussed; the solution is applied to other similar problems.

A problem is identified, followed by a proposal for solving the problem; benefits and drawbacks of the proposal are discussed; examples of the benefits and drawbacks are described; a challenge to the proposal is introduced and the proposal is rejected.

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, the group of Northern Utes mentioned in the third sentence of the fourth paragraph would be likely to believe each of the following statements EXCEPT:

choices.text: Standardizing traditional languages requires arbitrary choices and is sometimes unnecessary.
Written languages should reflect one standard dialect rather than several dialects.
Traditional languages can be taught even if they are not rigorously standardized.
Variant spellings of words are acceptable in a language if their meanings are clear.
The extent to which a language should be standardized depends upon a community’s needs.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following most accurately describes the author's attitude toward the goal of having a written language exactly match its oral equivalent?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
If we scan/search for "equivalent", we'll see it show up twice in the 3rd paragraph.

The 3rd paragraph says that a community may have difficulty writing down elements of a language "that has been primarily oral for centuries, as is often the case with traditional languages".

There might be a lack of acceptable written equivalents for certain sounds in that language. And if you insist that "every sound in the language have a unique written equivalent", you're setting yourself up for problems.

That's "a desirable but ultimately frustrating condition that no written language has ever fully satisfied."

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body: So it sounds like the author would say the goal of having a written language exactly match its oral equivalent is an understandable goal that is probably doomed to frustration and futility.

choices.text: conviction that an exact match is all but impossible to achieve
choices.explanation:
This matches up decently with the end of the 3rd paragraph, where the author says that when you try to get every sound in the language to have a unique written equivalent, it is a "desirable **but ultimately frustrating condition that no written language has ever fully satisfied**".

The language of "all but impossible" is very strong, but so is our support sentence, which says that no written language has **ever** been able to exactly match its oral equivalent.

choices.text: doubt that an exact match is worthy of consideration even in principle
choices.explanation:
In that final sentence of the 3rd paragraph, the author acknowledges the appeal of wanting a written language to match up perfectly with its oral counterpart.

She says it's "a **desirable** condition". So she seems to think that it's worth of consideration in principle. She just thinks it's a fool's errand, in practice.

choices.text: faith that an exact match is attainable if certain obstacles are eliminated
choices.tag: Out of Scope: exact match attainable
choices.explanation: This sounds far too optimistic that we could ever have an exact match, given that the author says that "no written language has ever fully" been able to. accomplish an exact match.

choices.text: confidence that an exact match can easily be accomplished in most languages
choices.explanation:
This is even more optimistic than (C), which was already too optimistic.

The author tells us that no language has ever been able to fully satisfy an exact match, so where would her confidence come from that in most languages an exact match can easily be accomplished.

choices.text: suspicion that the motives behind the attempts to achieve the goal are not entirely benevolent
choices.explanation:
Since the author acknowledges that having an exact match is a "desirable condition", it doesn't sound like she's suspicious of people who want an exact match.

She seems to be saying, "I totally get your motives. Unfortunately, what you're asking for seems to be impossible since no written language has ever pulled it off".

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, which one of the following appears to be a principle guiding the actions of those attempting to preserve their traditional languages?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
It's pretty hard to anticipate the answer to any Principle question in RC. They are sort of like Necessary Assumptions that underlie something we were told.

Because of that, we want to avoid picking an answer whose wording seems overly strong, and our correct answer, if negated, should feel like it goes against the passage in some way.

The keywords here are "people attempting to preserve their traditional language". The passage was mainly about tribal communities in North America, but these keywords refer to **anyone** attempting to preserve a traditional language.

Thus, if we're hunting first for supporting sentences, we would want to find a detail that sounds like a broad fact of the matter, rather than one specific to a certain tribe.

The 2nd paragraph starts off with a promising universal:

*before **any** community can systematically and formally teach a traditional language to its younger members, it must first document the language's grammar ... the grammatical info is then arranged in sequence from simpler to more complex, and methods are devised to present the sequence in ways that will be most useful and appropriate to the culture.*

Alright so let's look for stuff like
1. document grammar first
2. go from simpler to more complex
3. devise methods that are appropriate to the culture

choices.text: In writing down an oral language, one should always be concerned primarily with the degree of correspondence between spoken sounds and written symbols.
choices.explanation:
This doesn't reinforce any of our Support Window from the 2nd paragraph. It sounds very extreme: *we should **always** be **primarily** concerned with matching spoken sounds to written symbols.*

And it seems to go against the 3rd paragraph's ending, in which the author says that it's basically a hopeless pursuit to try to get every sound in the language to have a unique correspondence with written symbols.

choices.text: In deciding whether and how to standardize and teach a primarily oral language, one should always keep the needs of the community and the culture foremost.
choices.explanation: The teaching methods should be useful and appropriate to the culture, and the Utes' flexible spellings made sense for their community's needs. Those statements support the community-centered principle. Evaluate that textual support directly rather than assume a modifier is harmless merely because it appears in every answer.

choices.text: In determining whether to preserve a language orally or preserve it in writing, one should always strive to ignore the influences of the majority culture and focus on which method is most effective.
choices.tag: Out of Scope: most effective / Contradicted: ignore influence
choices.explanation: The defenders write their languages because oral traditions are declining, and concede that oral preservation is possible if the relevant outside pressures are resisted. Their choice therefore takes majority-culture effects into account. The passage does not establish a general preference for oral over written preservation, or advise ignoring those effects.

choices.text: In considering how to present the grammar of a primarily oral language to students, one should always employ a sequence that tackles more difficult concepts first.
choices.explanation:
This goes against the 2nd part of our Support Window

1. document grammar first
**2. go from simpler to more complex**
3. devise methods that are appropriate to the culture

This is saying to tackle difficult concepts first.

choices.text: In adjudicating among variant spellings of words from different language traditions, one should always favor the spelling preferred by the majority of the community.
choices.explanation:
In the 4th paragraph, we hear that the Northern Utes decided not to standardize their language, "agreeing that **various phonetic spellings** would be accepted as long as their meanings were clear".

This answer is saying that you shouldn't accept variant spellings. You should pick the one that the majority uses.

passages.title: Platypus Bill
passages.text:
Scientists have long known that the soft surface of the bill of the platypus is perforated with openings that contain sensitive nerve endings. Only recently, however, have biologists concluded on the basis of new evidence that the animal uses its bill to locate its prey while underwater, a conclusion suggested by the fact that the animal’s eyes, ears, and nostrils are sealed when it is submerged. The new evidence comes from neurophysiological studies, which have recently revealed that within the pores on the bill there are two kinds of sensory receptors: mechanoreceptors, which are tiny pushrods that respond to tactile pressure, and electroreceptors, which respond to weak electrical fields. Having discovered that tactile stimulation of the pushrods sends nerve impulses to the brain, where they evoke an electric potential over an area of the neocortex much larger than the one stimulated by input from the limbs, eyes, and ears, Bohringer concluded that the bill must be the primary sensory organ for the platypus. Her finding was supported by studies showing that the bill is extraordinarily sensitive to tactile stimulation: stimulation with a fine glass stylus sent a signal by way of the fifth cranial nerve to the neocortex and from there to the motor cortex. Presumably nerve impulses from the motor cortex then induced a snapping movement of the bill. But Bohringer’s investigations did not explain how the animal locates its prey at a distance.

Scheich’s neurophysiological studies contribute to solving this mystery. His initial work showed that when a platypus feeds, it swims along steadily wagging its bill from side to side until prey is encountered. It thereupon switches to searching behavior, characterized by erratic movements of the bill over a small area at the bottom of a body of water, which is followed by homing in on the object and seizing it. In order to determine how the animal senses prey and then distinguishes it from other objects on the bottom, Scheich hypothesized that a sensory system based on electroreception similar to that found in sharks might exist in the platypus. In further experiments he found he could trigger the switch from patrolling to searching behavior in the platypus by creating a dipole electric field in the water with the aid of a small 1.5-volt battery. The platypus, sensitive to the weak electric current that was created, rapidly oriented toward the battery at a distance of 10 centimeters and sometimes as much as 30 centimeters. Once the battery was detected, the platypus would inevitably attack it as if it were food. Scheich then discovered that the tail flicks of freshwater shrimp, a common prey of the platypus, also produce weak electric fields and elicit an identical response. Scheich and his colleagues believe that it is reasonable to assume that all the invertebrates on which the platypus feeds must produce electric fields.

summaries.standard:
**Passage Summary**

**Topic**

How the platypus uses its bill—specifically, touch and electroreception—to find prey underwater.

**Framework**

Old / New

**Main Point**

Scientists long knew the bill contained sensitive nerve endings; recent studies reveal that it relies on both touch and electric signals to hunt underwater prey, since its eyes, ears, and nostrils are sealed while submerged.
*Most Valuable Sentence*: "Only recently, however, have biologists concluded on the basis of new evidence that the animal uses its bill to locate its prey while underwater" (second sentence of P1).

**P1: Discovery of Bill Sensory Function**

Scientists have long known that the platypus's bill is full of nerves, but only recently concluded that it is the primary way the animal finds food underwater because it can sense both touch and electrical signals. Bohringer's studies showed the bill is super sensitive to touch, but didn’t explain how it locates prey they can’t touch yet.

**P2: Electroreception Revealed Through Experiments**

Scheich’s research showed that platypuses hunt by detecting weak electric fields, just like some fish. His experiments (using a battery in water) made platypuses react as if food were present, showing they can sense electric fields from a distance—which led to the idea that the platypus hunts by sensing the electrical signals of its prey.

questions.prompt: The primary purpose of the passage is to

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The passage begins with some classic *Old / New* clues:
*Scientists have **long known** X.*
*Only **recently, however**, have biologists concluded Y.*

This new finding is that the platypus uses its bill to locate its prey while underwater.

In any Old / New passage, we're curious how the author feels about this New idea. Is she resisting it? Celebrating it? Elaborating on it?

The passage doesn't contain any sort of rebuttal or pushback to this idea. The author just spills out lots of specific details to elaborate on this new finding.

The headline is that the platypus uses its bill to locate prey while underwater.

The passage then subdivides based on the fact that the platypus's bill contains two different type of receptors: mechanoreceptors and electroreceptors.

The remainder of the 1st paragraph explains how important a sensory organ the bill is and how mechanoreceptors trigger a snapping movement of the bill to eat nearby prey.

The 2nd paragraph deals with the electroreceptors, which explain how the platypus can sense prey at a distance (even though its' eyes, ears, and nostrils are sealed).

Overall, the purpose seems to be "to present what we now know about how the platypus uses its bill to locate prey while underwater".

choices.text: explain how the platypus locates prey at a distance
choices.explanation:
This explains the function of the 2nd paragraph, but not the passage overall. The 1st paragraph explicitly does *not* explain how the platypus locates prey at a distance.

But the 1st paragraph is still an important part (1/2) of the passage. In that paragraph, we learn that it is a new / recent discovery that the platypus uses its bill to locate prey.

It uses mechanoreceptors to feel out prey within touching distance (1st paragraph) and electroreceptors to sense prey at a distance (2nd paragraph).

We need an answer that could better wrap its arms around both paragraphs.

choices.text: present some recent scientific research on the function of the platypus’s bill
choices.explanation:
If we saw this passage as *Old / New*, then we would certainly find some of this answer's wording attractive:
*present some **recent** research*

Is the research dealing with the function of the bill? Yes, it deals with how the platypus uses its bill to locate prey underwater.

We might not love that this answer sounds a little too broad in saying "the function of the platypus's bill", given that the passage is only telling us about one specific function (locating prey underwater).

After all, the platypus's bill may have many functions. But it's still true to say that we are hearing the takeaways of people who were researching the function of the platypus's bill. In fact, one takeaway is that "the platypus's bill functions as **the primary sense organ** of the platypus."

Mostly, we just have to come to peace with this answer being the best available, despite being imperfect.

choices.text: assess the results of Bohringer’s experimental work about the platypus
choices.tag: Out of Scope: assess / Too Narrow: Bohringer
choices.explanation:
We can stop reading with the verb "assess", which implies that the author evaluated the merits of Bohringer's work.

This author was purely in presentational / reporting mode. He didn't do any editorializing. We can't find his opinion anywhere.

Also, Bohringer's work only covers the 1st paragraph. What about Scheich's work?

choices.text: present Scheich’s contributions to scientific work about the platypus
choices.explanation:
It is true that the passage presents Scheich's contributions, but this only covers the 2nd paragraph. This answer would essentially have the same virtues and detriments as choice (A).

We want an answer broad enough to envelop both the 1st and 2nd paragraphs.

choices.text: describe two different kinds of pores on the platypus’s bill
choices.explanation:
The passage doesn't describe two different kinds of pores on the bill. It defines two different kinds of receptors within pores on the bill.

However, even if this answer said 'receptors' instead of 'pores', it would still feel too narrow.

The author's main objective in writing the passage wasn't to define two different types of receptors. The author was trying to report on our new discovery that the platypus uses its bill to locate prey underwater.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following statements best expresses the main idea of the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Anticipate
explanationBlocks.body:
The central topic of the passage was the platypus's bill.

The framework we probably used was *Old / New,* because the passage begins with these two thoughts:
*Scientists have **long known** X.*
*Only **recently, however**, have biologists concluded Y.*

Or maybe we used *Highlight Noteworthy*, since the passage feels so informative and presentational.

What is the new thought that the passage wants to highlight about the platypus's bill?

We just figured out that **the platypus uses its bill to locate its prey while underwater.**

Let's start by making sure the main clause of our main point answer reflects that key headline idea, and then see if we can sign off on all the other details within the answer choice.

choices.text: Neurophysiological studies have established that the bill of the platypus is one of its primary sensory organs.
choices.explanation: Although this *was* said in the 1st paragraph, the main takeaway is supposed to be that "the bill of the platypus is used to locate prey underwater".

choices.text: Neurophysiological studies have established that the platypus uses its bill to locate its prey underwater.
choices.explanation:
Okay, not too shabby!

This aligns with our Most Valuable Sentence, which was adorned with two of the famous Purpose Pivots (but, yet, **however, recently**).

Everything else in the passage was subsidiary to this headline. It elaborated on exactly how it is that the platypus uses its bill to locate prey underwater.

choices.text: Bohringer’s neurophysiological studies have established that sensory receptors in the bill of the platypus respond to electrical stimulation.
choices.tag: Wrong Emphasis: respond to stimulation / Too Narrow: Bohringer / Mismatched Scientists
choices.explanation:
The passage is pretty well split between Bohringer and Scheich, so we wouldn't want our main point answer to only mention one of them.

This answer fails to present the main discovery: *the platypus uses its bill to locate prey underwater*.

Instead, it just presents a very minor narrow detail. It also botches the detail, in the sense that Scheich, not Bohringer, is the scientist who worked on electrical stimulation.

Bohringer worked on tactile stimluation.

choices.text: Biologists have concluded that the surface of the bill of the platypus is perforated with openings that contain sensitive nerve endings.
choices.explanation:
Although this *was* said in the 1st paragraph, the main takeaway is supposed to be that "the bill of the platypus is used to locate prey underwater".

How does the platypus use its bill to locate prey underwater?

*Well, it starts with knowing that the surface of the bill is perforated with pores that contain two different types of receptors ....*

This answer is just presenting a subsidiary detail.

choices.text: Biologists have concluded that the hunting platypus responds to weak electric fields emitted by freshwater invertebrates.
choices.explanation:
Although this *was* said in the 2nd paragraph, the main takeaway is supposed to be that "the bill of the platypus is used to locate prey underwater".

Part of how it hunts prey underwater is picking up on their weak electric field to detect it at a distance.

Once it picks up the electrical "scent", then it dive bombs the bottom of the water and starts throwing its bill around. From the 1st paragraph, we know that if the bill knocks up against anything, that tactile pressure induces the bill to start a snapping motion, to gobble up whatever is nearby.

Like (D), this provides one subsidiary detail in the overarching story about the platypus using its bill to hunt prey underwater.

questions.prompt: During the studies supporting Bohringer's finding, as they are described in the passage, which one of the following occurred before a nerve impulse reached the motor cortex of the platypus?

choices.text: The electroreceptors sent the nerve impulse to the fifth cranial nerve.
The neocortex induced a snapping movement of the bill.
The mechanoreceptors sent the nerve impulse via the fifth cranial nerve to the electroreceptors.
The platypus opened the pores on its bill.
The fifth cranial nerve carried the nerve impulse to the neocortex.

questions.prompt: Which one of the following strategies is most similar to Scheich's experimental strategy as it is described in the passage?

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
Scheich has a hypothesis that the platypus has a sensory system based on electroreception, similar to that found in sharks.

His experiment involves creating an electric field in the water using a battery (with the logic being that **if** the platypus has electroreception and can detect electricity in the water, then it would detect the weak electric presence of the battery).

The platypus did indeed sense the battery and attack it as though it were food. We later discover that the tail flick of shrimp (a common prey of the platypus) produces an electric field similar to that of the battery.

It's hard to know which of these aspects the correct answer will reinforce, but we have several traits we could look for:

- hypothesizing that X has a certain trait because it's known that Y has that trait (maybe the platypus can sense electricity, since sharks can)

- using something artificial to simulate something natural (the 1.5 volt battery simulates the electric field of the shrimp)

choices.text: To determine the mating habits of birds, a biologist places decoys near the birds’ nests that resemble the birds and emit bird calls.
choices.explanation: This proposal studies mating behavior using both a bird-shaped decoy and bird calls. Scheich instead tests a particular prey-detection sense with an artificial source of the relevant physical signal. C preserves that hypothesis-and-signal structure more closely.

choices.text: To determine whether certain animals find their way by listening for echoes to their cries, a biologist plays a tape of the animals’ cries in their vicinity.
choices.explanation: Playing an animal's cries is not itself a test of whether it navigates by listening to echoes returning from those cries. Scheich tests detection of a signal associated with prey. C more directly pairs a hypothesized prey-detection sense with an artificial source of its signal.

choices.text: To determine whether an animal uses heat sensitivity to detect prey, a biologist places a heat-generating object near the animal’s home.
choices.explanation:
This again sounds like our second quality.

- hypothesizing that X has a certain trait because it's known that Y has that trait

**- using something artificial to simulate something natural**

This match is stronger than the other though for a couple reasons:

1. the hypothesis relates to being able to sense a certain property emitted by prey (in Scheich's experiment, the prey emits an electric field, and he's testing whether the platypus can detect the electric field). Here, we think an animal can detect a prey's heat.

2. the artificial object isn't a close facsimile of the prey animal. It's just something that emits the property being tested. In Scheich's experiment, a battery was used to generate an electric field. In this one, a heat-generating object is used to generate heat.

choices.text: A fisherman catches fish by dangling in the water rubber replicas of the fishes’ prey that have been scented with fish oil.
choices.explanation:
This isn't even an experiment. This is just luring fish by giving them an artificial object that is designed to be a close replica of the natural object.

It's visually similar and smells similar.

Even if this were an experiment, it would only test whether fish could tell the difference between their actual prey and an object disguised to look and smell like their prey.

choices.text: A game warden captures an animal by baiting a cage with a piece of meat that the animal will want to eat.
choices.explanation:
This also isn't an experiment. This is just luring animals with the actual food they want to eat.

In Schiech's experiment, we don't think the platypus actually wants to eat a 1.5 volt battery. It's just sensing something emitted by the battery, which is also emitted by the platypus's prey.

questions.prompt: It can be inferred from the passage that during patrolling behavior, the platypus is attempting to

explanationBlocks.heading: Research
explanationBlocks.body:
In the beginning of the 2nd paragraph we're told,

*When a platypus feeds, it swims along steadily wagging its bill from side to side until prey is encountered. It thereupon **switches** to searching behavior.*

And in the sentence about "patrolling", we hear another reference to that switch:

*In further experiments he found he could trigger the **switch** from patrolling behavior to searching behavior.*

So apparently "patrolling behavior" refers to the first half of that previous sentence: *swimming along steadily wagging its bill from side to side until prey is encountered*.

Let's look for the closest match for that. In patrolling behavior, **the platypus is attempting to ...** "encounter/find prey".

choices.text: capture prey that it has detected
choices.explanation:
We're looking for "attempting to **locate** prey", and this is saying "attempting to capture prey that it has detected".

First, it's on patrol, looking for prey.

Once it encounters prey, it **switches** out of patrolling mode and into searching mode. So this answer seems to describe searching mode.

choices.text: distinguish one kind of prey from another
choices.explanation: The passage describes detecting prey and distinguishing it from other objects, not distinguishing one kind of prey from another. Patrolling precedes the localized searching and capture sequence. The claimed comparison among prey types is unsupported.

choices.text: detect electric fields produced by potential prey
choices.explanation:
We're looking for "attempting to **locate** prey", and this and (E) are the two answers that convey the idea of trying to locate prey.

So then we have to ask ourselves, does a platypus locate prey by detecting electric fields (C), or by picking up the scent (E)?

The 2nd paragraph is telling us that the platypus detects the electric field of its prey. That's how in the experiment they were able to attract a platypus using a 1.5 volt battery.

choices.text: stimulate its mechanoreceptors
choices.explanation:
The mechanoreceptors are what is used for tactile pressure, once the platypus has switched into searching mode and is homing in on the object and seizing it.

The electroreceptors are what the platypus is using during the patrolling phase, as it tries to detect prey by picking up on their electric field.

choices.text: pick up the scent of its prey
choices.explanation:
We're looking for "attempting to **locate** prey", and this and (C) are the two answers that convey the idea of trying to locate prey.

So then we have to ask ourselves, does a platypus locate prey by detecting electric fields (C), or by picking up the scent (E)?

The 2nd paragraph is telling us that the platypus detects the electric field of its prey. That's how in the experiment they were able to attract a platypus using a 1.5 volt battery. The platypus likely can't smell anything underwater, especially given that "its eyes, ears, and **nostrils** are sealed when it is submerged" (2nd sentence of passage).
